newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stocks seen with limited downside.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stocks seen with limited downside.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks were tipped to retreat further this week, but confidence in underlying market fundamentals could limit any downside, analysts said.
"It is possible we could see the index fall to the 13,000 level or slightly lower," said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities. "I am a little worried about the U.S. bond market."
The outlook, however, also depends on whether Friday's 102-point surge on Wall Street is sustained this week.
The Hang Seng Index closed 19.35 points higher at 13,222.79 on Friday after a week in which bullish local market sentiment was shaken hard by inflation fears in the United States.
The index shed 181.35 points or 1.35 percent over the holiday-shortened week. Turnover was brisk, averaging HK$10.32 billion ($1.33 billion) a day in the three full trading days.
"Once the bond yield rises, people talk about a (U.S.) interest rate hike again," said Ng.
The U.S. long bond yield closed Friday's trading in New York at 6.73 percent, slightly lower than Thursday's 6.74 percent, but this was higher than pre-New Year's trading of 6.64 percent.

But as Hong Kong's economy picks up, with the key property sector robust, and the market's growing exposure to China's economic expansion not fully discounted, investors remained confident over the fundamental outlook, brokers said.

Brokers also said the local market -- with its growing weight in so-called red chips, H-shares and other China-related stocks -- was expected to gradually decouple from U.S. market trends, but that day had not yet arrived.
While blue chips turned sluggish in late December, in line with Wall Street, China-related issues remained relatively robust until they hit profit-taking on Friday, they added.
"More China operations are being injected into Hong Kong red chips," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong. "So (earnings) growth is coming from well beyond Hong Kong."
In the short term, however, the market is heading for some consolidation and could struggle around the 13,000 level, Wong said.

"Underlying sentiment in Hong Kong is strong, and we far from discount the possibility of 'decoupling' in 1997, but against this must be weighed the weakness of the U.S. bond market," said John Schofield, regional technical analyst at NAVA SC Securities.
Schofield said a further rise in the long bond yield to 6.95 percent is possible. "So a little short-term caution is in order for Hong Kong," he added.

Other technical analysts said the charts were giving mixed signals. The daily chart points to the market trying to find a bottom around the 13,000 level, said Ted Chen, technical analyst at Technical Data Inc.
"The longer term outlook is pretty good even if the index corrects back to 12,800," Chen added. "That would be a good buying opportunity."
